analytics — codebase report

Built 2026-11-10 at commit 0c3903a941

Plausible Analytics is a web analytics service. Its server is an Elixir and Phoenix app. A small JavaScript tracker script sends page views to it, and a React dashboard reads the reports. The repo holds 2,141 files and 715,880 lines, with 4,476 commits since 2019-09-02. Postgres stores accounts and sites, and ClickHouse stores events and sessions. A newcomer should start with lib/plausible_web/router.ex, then follow one pageview through the ingestion code and one report through the stats code. All 15 charts are present. The module import chart covers only JavaScript and TypeScript, because the measurement skips Elixir imports.

The stack

The browser sends events to the Phoenix web layer. The Elixir core turns them into sessions and writes batches to ClickHouse. Account data lives in Postgres, and the Oban workers (a background job library) call Google Analytics 4, send email and write imported rows. Start here to see which part talks to which.

Recording a pageview

The tracker script posts to /api/event, which ExternalController handles. The ingestion code builds a request, asks GateKeeper if the site may send events, and runs the event through a list of steps. Any step can drop the event. A kept event goes to the session cache, then to the event write buffer, which flushes to ClickHouse. The controller answers 202 once the event is buffered, and also when a step dropped it; an invalid event gets 400.

Loading a dashboard report

The dashboard posts a query to /api/stats/:domain/query. A plug checks that the user may see the site. StatsController parses the parameters and builds a Query, which runs through a chain of checks. QueryRunner then optimizes the query, builds SQL and reads the rows from ClickHouse. The controller sends the result back as JSON.

How an event joins a session

The session cache looks up a session by user id, then by the previous salt user id. An engagement event only refreshes a session that exists, and is dropped if there is none. Any other event updates the found session or starts a new one. An update writes the old row with sign -1 and the new row with sign 1, so ClickHouse can collapse the rows. A cached session is reused only if it is at most 30 minutes old.

Data model across Postgres and ClickHouse

Postgres holds the account side: teams, users, memberships, subscriptions, sites, goals and site imports. A team owns many sites and has one subscription. ClickHouse holds events_v2 and sessions_v2, which link to a site by site_id. The chart lists only the columns that carry the relations and a few key fields.

Plausible routes

The router has public pages, signed-in pages and HTTP APIs. Public pages are register, login and shared dashboards. Signed-in pages cover the site list, new site, installation, the site dashboard, settings and billing. User settings include guest sites, API keys and connected apps. The APIs include the events API, the internal stats API, the public stats API v1 and v2, and the plugins API. The sites API under /api/v1/sites is compiled only in the enterprise build.

Site import lifecycle

A site import has four statuses: pending, importing, completed and failed. A new import starts as pending, and the worker moves it to importing when the job starts. It ends as completed if all rows are imported, or failed on an error or when Oban discards the job. A rate limit, socket or server error from GA4 keeps it importing and resumes it 65 minutes later, and a crashed job with retries left purges its rows and runs again.

Adding a first site

The chart follows a site owner from sign-up to the first dashboard view. The email activation step and the tracker script step are the weakest, with scores of 3 and 2. The site status moves from new_site through verification_succeeded and first_pageview to completed. Installation support, a headless browser check in the tracker folder, verifies the script.

Importing Google Analytics 4 data

The user picks a property and dates. The controller clamps the dates, creates a pending import and rejects the request if another import runs. The Oban worker fetches the GA4 reports and writes rows to ClickHouse through a buffer. On success it marks the import completed and emails the user; on error it purges the imported rows, marks it failed and emails the user. A rate limit, socket or server error from GA4 is not drawn: it keeps the rows, sends no email and resumes the same import 65 minutes later.
